title: COP31 enters final week with finance and fossil fuels unresolved as ministers arrive
dek: A first draft of the summit's main decision is due early this week in Antalya. Developing countries want adaptation finance tripled and a funded just transition mechanism; the presidency is pushing an electrification pledge India has refused to sign.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The UN climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, entered its second and final week on Monday with ministers arriving to settle disputes over money, adaptation and fossil fuels that negotiators failed to resolve in the first week. A first draft of the conference's main "cover decision" is expected early in the week, and the talks are scheduled to end on Friday, 20 November.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell called the first week's progress "constructive" but urged governments to "move swiftly to the hardest issues", according to reports. A stocktaking plenary on Saturday night, chaired jointly by Türkiye and Australia, was expected to show countries' first red lines.

## Where the talks stand

The conference's draft cover text is still a list of all the proposals parties have made rather than a negotiated draft, according to reports from Antalya. The main disputes are:

- Adaptation: African countries want a commitment to triple finance for adapting to climate change to at least $120 billion a year by 2035, an option included in a draft on the global goal on adaptation. Another option would reopen elements of the finance target agreed at COP30 last year, which African countries are expected to resist.
- Just transition: a draft note proposes a two-tier "just transition mechanism" whose outputs would mostly be a knowledge hub, reports and an annual meeting, with "matchmaking" of requests to existing support rather than new money. Campaigners called it weak; developing countries want grant-based finance and technology transfer.
- Fossil fuels: a proposal to welcome Brazil's voluntary roadmap for transitioning away from coal, oil and gas is in the draft cover decision. A new climate finance work programme remained stalled at the end of the first week.

Some countries, including Arab states, Mexico, South Korea and Switzerland, have also proposed holding the conferences every two years instead of every year.

## What the hosts say

"We aim to deliver a strong outcome in Antalya through ministerial-level talks next week," Türkiye's environment minister and COP31 president, Murat Kurum, told a briefing on Saturday, according to reports. "We will turn pledges into decisions that make a tangible difference in people's lives." Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, who is president of the negotiations under a hosting compromise, said the aim was "the most ambitious outcome possible through consensus", the reports said.

Türkiye's flagship initiative is a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of global energy use from about 20% today to 35% by 2035. The European Union has asked for "clean" electrification, a term that could reopen the fight over fossil fuels, though its negotiator Wopke Hoekstra hinted the bloc might drop the demand to win wider support, according to reports. Some large developing countries have pushed back against such sectoral targets.

## India's position

India has said it will not sign the electrification pledge or back any roadmap to phase out fossil fuels. "We are not going to sign any pledge. This is their agenda," Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav told reporters in New Delhi before the conference, according to reports. At the leaders' summit last week India pressed developed countries to meet their legal obligation to provide climate finance, while UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that current national plans put the world on course for more than 2.5°C of warming.

## What happens next

Ministers and heads of delegation will negotiate on the draft texts through the week. A final package has to be agreed by consensus of the 197 parties to the UN climate convention and the EU before the scheduled close on Friday; COP talks often run over into the weekend.
